invariants.rule: Publication-state flag. Placeholder/stub chapters are `indexed: false`; published chapters with real content are `indexed: true`. Both states must be explicit and set on every chapter — never omit it. PRIMARY PURPOSE: draft-release-notes.mjs emits a "chapter added" entry when a chapter transitions from false to true, so leaving a real chapter fieldless breaks that explicit false→true signal. SECONDARY EFFECT: consumers read `indexed !== false`, so `indexed: false` also keeps stub ("coming soon") chapters out of the verse search index (build-verse-index.mjs), out of the sitemap, and robots-noindex’d (see shouldIndex in [slug].astro) — desired, since placeholder pages should not be searchable. The chapter validator additionally uses `indexed: false` to recognize a stub and skip its "no verse markers" check, so stubs must carry it. For a real chapter, `true` and absent behave identically in both consumers; `true` is required only to keep the release-notes lifecycle an explicit two-state (false→true) machine rather than one relying on field absence.

Each verse marker id (id="vN" on <sup class="vn">) must appear exactly once per chapter. A verse that spans a paragraph break keeps its marker only at its start; the continuation paragraph carries NO marker (this is what makes the number appear once). Duplicate ids are invalid HTML — epubcheck rejects them and the #vN deep-link anchor becomes ambiguous — so a repeated verse number is always a bug, never a style choice. The chapter validator enforces uniqueness as an error (any verse id appearing more than once fails validation and blocks the pre-commit hook).

A verse marker id is exactly "v" + digits. Suffixed forms (id="v41b") are rejected. They existed in john-7 and john-8 as a way to re-show a verse number on a continuation paragraph while slipping past unique_verse_ids, and every consumer matches id="v(\d+)", so the suffixed marker was invisible to all of them: the verse split in build-verse-index left its digits in the extracted text as a stray number (and in the search vocabulary as the words "11" and "41"), addOsisIds gave it no data-osis, rewriteVerseIdsAndAnchors left an un-namespaced id on the Reading Mode page, and extractVerseTexts dropped the continuation chunk so an edit to it was reported against the FOLLOWING verse in the apps' Translation Updates feed. The convention is the one unique_verse_ids already states — a continuation paragraph carries no marker (187 such paragraphs across 76 published chapters). To let a reader share just part of a verse, link the block's own id (see "Sharing part of a verse" in CLAUDE.md); no marker is needed for that.

Prose in `paragraphs` and `footnotes[].html` uses Unicode curly quotes only — “ ” for quotations, ‘ ’ for nested quotations, and ’ for apostrophes and possessives. Straight ASCII quotes (U+0022, U+0027) are rejected. HTML attributes are exempt: the validator strips tags before checking, so `id="john-3-p1"` is fine while `it's` and "quoted" in the text are not. This is an ERROR, not a warning, because warnings fail neither CI nor the pre-commit hook — the predecessor rule was a footnote-only warning for straight DOUBLE quotes, and under it 439 straight quotes accumulated across 96 chapters (297 in footnotes, 90 in scripture paragraphs, plus 52 in drafts) before the 2026-08 cleanup converted them. Paragraphs are in scope precisely because they were the gap: straight quotes in the translation text itself were never checked. Mind the two-way risk when authoring — a straight quote is also easy to pair wrongly with a curly one (‘word" or "word’), which reads as a mismatched pair rather than a missing curl. ENTITY FORMS COUNT: `"` `'` `"` `'` `"` `'` are rejected too. They survive any literal-character scan while still decoding to a straight quote in the rendered page and in public/search/verses.json, which is exactly how 19 of them hid through the first pass of the 2026-08 cleanup. Prime notation is NOT a quote and must not be written with either form: the chiasm labels in 1corinthians-11 fn-b use U+2032 PRIME (A B C D D′ C′ B′ A′), which states what they are and keeps them outside this rule instead of needing an exemption.

Curly double quotes must balance WITHIN each footnote. A footnote is a self-contained editorial object — a reader meets it whole, in a popover or at the foot of the chapter — so a quotation it opens is one it must also close. The check strips tags, counts U+201C against U+201D, and errors on a mismatch. DOUBLES ONLY: a curly ’ is an apostrophe far more often than it is a nested closer, so singles cannot be counted this way and are not. WHY IT EXISTS: this one cheap rule found every defect of the 2026-08 shared-note cleanup. Five copies of the hupotasso note (1corinthians-14 fn-bb, ephesians-5 fn-r, hebrews-2 fn-h, james-4 fn-n, titus-2 fn-k) had lost the closing ” of their quotation from TDNT, and no master-vs-repo diff could ever have raised it, because the note is one editorial object stored in nine places and BOTH sides were fragmented — there was no undamaged copy to diff against. The same scan surfaced seven wrong-direction pairs (‘lord” — well-formed to any straight-quote scan, a mismatched pair to a reader) in six further chapters. Note the limit: this counts, it does not pair, so a note whose quotes balance while running the wrong direction still passes. That defect class is documented in CLAUDE.md and has no automated check.

The <sup class="fn-ref"> anchors must appear in the paragraphs in the same order as the entries of footnotes[], with no label anchored twice. Footnote labels are POSITIONAL (a…z, then aa…zz, then aaa…), so the sequence is the whole meaning of a label: out of order, a reader following the letters reads the notes in an order the author did not write. The pre-existing referential check proves that every anchor RESOLVES to a footnote and that every footnote is anchored somewhere, which is a different claim entirely — 2corinthians-5 shipped fn-f and fn-g transposed (document order e g f h) with every link working perfectly, endemeo explaining "out of our homeland" and ekdemeo explaining "in our homeland", exactly backwards. Fixing it meant swapping BOTH the note bodies and the two anchors, so that each note stayed attached to the word it explains. Duplicates are folded into the same rule because they break the same thing from the other end: two anchors sharing an id make the #fnref-X return link ambiguous and put the same letter in the text twice.

A verse marker must be preceded by whitespace, or open its block. sup.vn is inline-block and NO CSS supplies a gap, so the space before the number has to be in the text; without it the marker welds to the preceding sentence and renders as "sheep.12 The". The corpus votes overwhelmingly for the separator (4,159 to 3 at the time the rule was written). ONE EXEMPTION: a paragraph opening a bracketed passage, where the ⟦ marker and its footnote anchor legitimately precede the first verse — that exemption lives at the VALIDATOR call site, not in findUnseparatedVerseMarkers, matching how the changelog handles the same shape. The rule reuses that shared helper rather than restating the boundary rule, since a second copy is the one way it could quietly stop agreeing with the tools that repair against it. TWO ORIGINS, and they need different remedies: a restore from a Word master drops the separator because the master has none to contribute (the verse span ends AT the next marker, so it owns that space) — repair-verse-separators.mjs fixed those; and the 2026-02 import lost two in matthew-12 where the master DOES have the space, which that script could not see, because it only repairs where the pre-restore revision had one.

A contested passage is wrapped in ⟦ (U+27E6) and ⟧ (U+27E7). The retired two-character forms `[|` and `|]` are rejected in `paragraphs` and `footnotes[].html`. The corpus moved to the real double brackets on 2026-09-05 — the standard critical-edition notation for text of doubtful authenticity — because `[|` reads on screen as a typo or a broken tag rather than as notation. THIS IS A REPO-ONLY CONVENTION, exactly like en_dash_numeric_ranges: the WORD MASTERS still carry `[|`/`|]`, so every route back into the corpus is live — an approved restore through scripts/reconcile/, a fresh `npm run import:chapter` of a bracketed book (the importer's whole guarantee is that it reproduces the master verbatim), or a hand-copy out of Word. WHY IT IS AN ERROR RATHER THAN A WARNING: an old-form marker is two ordinary ASCII characters, so it renders to a reader as a literal "[|" AND survives every plain-text extractor that is not looking for it — the search index, the apps' Translation Updates feed, Copy verse / Share, the glossary alignment scan. stripBracketMarkers in src/lib/bracket-markers.mjs deliberately still strips BOTH forms, so an escape is harmless rather than reader-visible; this rule is what keeps the corpus itself single-form. The six passages are Mark 16:9–20, John 7:53–8:11, John 9:38–39a, John 11:28–32, Romans 16:24 and Romans 16:25–27.

No directly adjacent, attribute-less, same-name tag seam (, ). Word splits a styled phrase at every run boundary, and those boundaries rarely fall on a word: the 2026-02 import carried in ekdemeo, and 187 seams like it across 47 files. They render CORRECTLY, which is why they hid for six months — the defect is not visual. It is that the corpus stops being searchable: a grep, a script, or a future Claude session looking for "ekdemeo" finds nothing, and a tooling guard written as /ekdemeo/.test(html) silently fails open. That is not hypothetical; it happened while fixing the 2corinthians-5 transposition above, and the fix was to test the tag-stripped text. ONLY attribute-less same-name seams count: two real anchors in a row are a legitimate shape (a word carrying two notes), and a seam with anything between it — even one space — is left alone, since `a b` is a different authoring choice from `a b`. Collapsing is provably safe: for every character of the stripped text, which formatting tags are open over it is unchanged, which is a stronger claim than the text being unchanged.

A numeric range takes an en dash — "Matthew 5:3–12", "verses 9–11" — never a hyphen. Settled corpus-wide 2026-08-20 (413 conversions across 111 files). THIS IS A REPO-ONLY CONVENTION and deliberately so: the Word masters keep hyphens, because Word autocorrects a dash between WORDS and does not autocorrect one between digits, so there is nothing on the master side to preserve and every restore from a master pulls individual ranges back toward the hyphen. Re-run the pass rather than fixing them one at a time. TWO EXCLUSIONS, both load-bearing: anything inside a tag (id="john-3-p1" is a hyphen and must stay one — the check splits on tags and scans only the text between them), and a URL printed as visible link text, where an en dash breaks the link a reader would type. The URL test is deliberately loose (a scheme, a leading www., or a token carrying a common TLD), since a false negative here costs a hyphen and a false positive costs a broken link.
